passages.title: The generator next door
passages.text:
For three years the family in the flat below ours ran a generator that sounded like a lorry idling in the corridor. It came on at dusk, when the public supply failed, and went off at midnight, when they went to bed. In between, we lived inside its noise. We raised our voices to talk, turned the television up until the neighbours on the other side complained, and learnt to sleep with pillows over our heads. The fumes came in through the kitchen window and settled on the curtains as a fine grey film.

We complained, of course. The man downstairs was polite and immovable. He had children who needed light to read by, a wife who sold frozen fish and could not afford to let the freezer thaw, and a father-in-law on oxygen. Everything he said was true, and none of it made the noise quieter. In the end we did what everyone in the street had done: we bought a generator of our own, and added our roar to his.

There are, by one estimate, more than twenty million small generators in Nigeria, and together they produce more electricity than the national grid supplies. Each is a private answer to a public failure. Nobody chose this arrangement; each household simply did the sensible thing, and the sum of twenty million sensible things is a country that cannot hear itself think.

passages.title: In defence of the mother tongue
passages.text:
A child who speaks Igbo at home arrives in Primary One and is taught to read in English, a language she has heard mainly on television. She must learn, at the same time, what a written word is and what the words mean. Her counterpart in a village school in Finland learns to read in Finnish, the language of her kitchen and her games, and meets English later, as a subject, when reading itself is no longer a mystery. It should surprise nobody which of the two reads more fluently at nine.

The argument for teaching young children in their mother tongue is not sentimental. Fifty years of research, including a famous six-year experiment in Ife in the 1970s, show that children taught in their own language in the early years learn to read faster, understand mathematics better and, when they eventually switch, learn English better too. What they gain is not a language but the habit of understanding.

The objections are practical rather than educational. Nigeria has more than five hundred languages, textbooks exist in only a handful, and many urban classrooms contain children from a dozen language groups. These are real difficulties. But they are reasons to begin carefully, not reasons to continue with a system in which a six-year-old is asked to climb two staircases at once.

passages.title: The tailor of Sabon Gari
passages.text:
Mallam Idris has sewn in the same shop in Sabon Gari for thirty-one years. The shop is a single room with a treadle machine, a mirror gone cloudy at the edges and a wall of brown-paper patterns, each labelled in pencil with a customer's name. He does not use a tape measure on regular customers; he looks at them, notes whether they have grown thicker or thinner since the last kaftan, and cuts. He is rarely wrong.

Business is not what it was. The market across the road now sells ready-made clothes from Turkey and China at prices he cannot match, and the young men who once queued before Sallah for a new babban riga now buy something off a hanger. Idris does not complain about this; he is a courteous man and, besides, he understands it. What he regrets is something else. 'A garment that is made for you,' he says, 'knows you. It knows that your left shoulder is lower. It knows that you sit a great deal. A garment from a hanger knows nobody.'

His son works in a bank in Kaduna and will not take over the shop. Idris has accepted this too. He has begun, in the slow afternoons, to teach a neighbour's boy who has shown an interest, and he cuts the boy's practice cloth from the paper patterns of customers who are long dead.

passages.title: Why drivers ignore the red light
passages.text:
Stand at any junction in Lagos at seven in the morning and count. In ten minutes you will see the red light run a dozen times, not by reckless boys on motorcycles but by sober men in company cars and mothers with children in the back seat. Ask them afterwards and they will not say that the light is unimportant. They will say that if they had stopped, the car behind would have hit them, or the car beside would have gone through and taken their place in the queue on the other side. They stop obeying the light because they believe that nobody else will.

This is the heart of the matter. A traffic light is not a fence; it cannot physically hold a car back. It works only as a shared expectation, and an expectation shared by half the drivers is no expectation at all. Every driver who runs the light teaches the drivers around him that the light is optional, and each of them teaches a dozen more. The disorder spreads faster than any warden can chase it.

The cure, then, is not a campaign of posters asking drivers to be patient. It is a short period in which the light is enforced so consistently, at a few junctions, that drivers come to expect that others will stop. Once that belief exists, it maintains itself, and the wardens can go elsewhere. Order in traffic, like most order, is a habit before it is a law.

passages.title: The boy who read on the bus
passages.text:
I noticed him because he was the only person on the bus who was not looking at a phone. He was perhaps fourteen, in a school uniform two sizes too large, and he was reading a paperback with its cover torn off, holding it close to his face because the light through the dirty windows was poor. When the bus lurched he did not look up. When the conductor shouted for fares he found his coins by touch. He turned a page as we passed the stadium, another at the roundabout, and by the time I got down at Ojota he had read, by my count, eleven pages in forty minutes of the worst traffic in the city.

I have thought about him often since, mostly with envy. I was once that boy. I read under the desk in class, in the bath, by torchlight after the generator went off. Somewhere between then and now, reading became a thing I did in short bursts between notifications, and I lost the ability to be so far inside a book that a bus could lurch without my noticing.

It is fashionable to say that young people no longer read. The boy on the bus is one piece of evidence against that claim, and I suspect there are many more. What has changed is not the young but the noise around them, and the boy had found, without anyone teaching him, the oldest defence against noise there is.

passages.title: The cost of a wedding
passages.text:
My cousin's wedding last December cost, by her father's reckoning, eleven million naira. There were two ceremonies and three outfits for the bride, a hall that seated eight hundred, a live band flown in from Lagos, and souvenirs - plastic buckets printed with the couple's faces - for every guest. Her father, a retired civil servant, sold a plot of land to pay for it. The couple began married life in a rented room, with a car loan and a debt to an uncle.

Nobody involved thought this strange. In much of Nigeria a wedding is not a private celebration but a public statement, and the statement is addressed less to the couple than to the community: we are people of substance; we have not been shamed. The eight hundred guests were the point. A smaller wedding would have been read as poverty, or quarrel, or worse.

I do not write this to mock my uncle, who loves his daughter and did what his neighbours would have done. I write it because the sum he spent would have bought the couple a two-bedroom flat in the same town, and because I suspect that most of the eight hundred, if they had been asked privately, would have preferred the couple to have the flat. Extravagance of this kind survives not because everyone wants it but because everyone believes that everyone else expects it.

passages.title: Rain from the roof
passages.text:
For six months of the year the sky over Calabar delivers, free of charge, more water than any household could use. It falls on roofs, runs into gutters, floods the streets and drains, unused, into the creeks. Then, for the other six months, the same households queue at boreholes and pay water vendors by the jerrycan. It is as if a man stood in a river in the wet season and died of thirst in the dry.

Harvesting rainwater is not new technology. A roof, a gutter, a pipe and a tank are all that is required, and our grandparents kept clay pots under the eaves for exactly this purpose. A roof of a hundred square metres in Calabar can collect more than two hundred thousand litres in a year - enough, with a modest tank and a little care, to carry a family through the dry months. The water needs only to be kept covered against mosquitoes and boiled, or filtered, before drinking.

Why, then, do so few houses do it? Partly because tanks cost money at the moment of building, when money is scarce, while the vendor's jerrycan costs money later, a little at a time. Partly because water that falls from the sky is not taken seriously; what is free is assumed to be worthless. And partly because no regulation requires it. A single clause in the building code - no roof without a tank - would do more for the city's water supply than another dozen boreholes.

passages.title: The answer sheet
passages.text:
The paper was folded into a square the size of a matchbox and passed to me under the desk during the Chemistry examination. I knew what it was without unfolding it. Kelechi, two rows in front, had a cousin who worked at a printing press, and for a week the hostel had talked of nothing else. I held it in my palm and did not open it, not because I was virtuous but because I was afraid; the invigilator that morning was Mr Ishola, who was said to be able to see through walls.

I passed Chemistry with a B. Kelechi and four others were caught in the Physics paper the following day, when the same cousin's answers turned out to be for a different set of questions, and all five wrote the same wrong answers in the same order. They were expelled. Kelechi's father, who had sold a cow to pay the fees, came to the school in a borrowed suit and wept in the principal's office.

I tell this story to my own students now, and I have learnt to tell it honestly. I did not refuse the paper; I merely failed to open it. The difference between Kelechi and me was not character but fear, and a school that relies on fear will produce, at best, students who cheat carefully. What I try to give them instead is the thing I did not have that morning: the certainty that I could pass on my own.

passages.title: Forty kilometres to a doctor
passages.text:
The nearest doctor to Kwakwa is forty kilometres away, on a road that becomes a river between June and September. The village has a health post, a two-room building with a nurse who visits on Tuesdays if her motorcycle is working, and a shelf of drugs that is full in January and empty by March. When a child convulses with fever at night, the family's choice is between a motorcycle ride in the dark with the child held between two adults, and a herbalist whose compound is at the end of the street.

It is easy, from a city, to condemn the choice of the herbalist. It is harder when one has seen the road. The mothers of Kwakwa are not ignorant; they know what a hospital can do, and they take their children there when they can. What they lack is not belief in medicine but access to it, and a system that expects a woman to carry a convulsing child forty kilometres has no right to lecture her about superstition.

The remedies are known and unglamorous. A community health worker who lives in the village and can give a first dose of anti-malarial at midnight; a drug supply that is refilled when it runs out rather than once a year; a road graded before the rains. None of these is a hospital, and none would make a headline. Together they would save more children in Kwakwa than a teaching hospital in the state capital ever will.

passages.title: Ninety minutes on plastic chairs
passages.text:
The viewing centre on our street is a shed of corrugated iron with sixty plastic chairs, two televisions and a generator that begins its shift ten minutes before kick-off. Admission is two hundred naira. On a Saturday evening when a Manchester club is playing, the chairs are full by six and the late-comers stand at the back, and the shed holds more concentrated emotion than any church in the district.

I used to regard the viewing centre as a symptom: of unemployment, of a nation watching other people's leagues because it had neglected its own, of young men with nothing better to do. I still think some of this is true. But I have sat in the shed often enough now to see something else. The men who fill it work: they are mechanics, conductors, tailors and hawkers, and the two hundred naira is earned. What they buy for it is ninety minutes in which the rules are clear, the referee is (mostly) fair, effort is rewarded and the outcome is not decided in advance by whom you know. It is hard to think of another place in their week where this is so.

The shed will empty at the final whistle and the men will go back to a city that is none of these things. But for ninety minutes they have lived, on plastic chairs, in a fairer world, and I have stopped believing that this is a waste of their time.

passages.title: Grandfather's barn
passages.text:
My grandfather's yam barn stood at the edge of the compound, a long frame of bamboo poles on which the tubers were tied in rows, largest at the bottom, so that a visitor could read a man's harvest at a glance. Every August the whole family gathered to tie the yams, and my grandfather walked the rows afterwards like a general inspecting troops. He knew, without counting, how many there were. He could tell, from the sound a tuber made when he tapped it, which would rot before Christmas.

The barn is gone now. My uncle, who inherited the land, grows cassava, which needs no barn, sells for more and can be harvested when money is needed rather than when the season says. He is not wrong. Yam is a demanding crop: it wants a rich soil, a mound for each tuber, a stake for each vine and a year of the farmer's attention. Cassava will grow in tired ground and wait in it, uncomplaining, for two years.

Yet something went with the barn that was not measured in naira. The tying of the yams was the one day in the year when every branch of the family was in the same place at the same time, and the barn was the family's account book, its pride and its insurance against hunger, standing in the open where anyone could see it. My uncle's cassava is sold in sacks and his money is in a bank, and neither can be walked along on an August afternoon.

passages.title: Two wheels
passages.text:
A bicycle costs less than a smartphone, needs no fuel, takes up a tenth of the road space of a car and is, over any distance under five kilometres in city traffic, faster than either a car or a bus. It produces no smoke and no noise, and the person riding it arrives having taken the exercise that the doctor keeps recommending. Given all this, the almost complete absence of bicycles from Nigerian cities requires explanation.

Part of the explanation is danger. A cyclist on Ikorodu Road shares the lane with articulated lorries and drivers who regard anything slower than themselves as an obstacle, and nobody should be surprised that few try it. Part is climate; nobody wishes to arrive at the office soaked. But the largest part, I suspect, is status. In much of the country the bicycle is the vehicle of the village messenger and the water seller, and to be seen on one is to announce that one cannot afford anything better. A young accountant would rather sit for two hours in a bus than pedal for twenty minutes past his colleagues.

Status is not permanent. Forty years ago the same was true in Amsterdam and Copenhagen, where the bicycle was for the poor until a generation decided otherwise, and today bankers cycle to work in suits. What changed there was not the weather but two things: lanes that made cycling safe, and a small number of visibly successful people who were seen to prefer it. The first is the government's job. The second is ours.

questions.C: was his own father's favourite crop
questions.D: needs a larger barn than yam does
questions.explanation: Cassava 'needs no barn, sells for more' and grows 'in tired ground', while yam 'wants... a year of the farmer's attention'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'uncomplaining' as used in the passage suggests that cassava
questions.A: makes no sound when it is harvested
questions.B: is a very difficult crop to grow
questions.D: is left in the ground and never harvested
questions.explanation: Cassava 'will grow in tired ground and wait in it, uncomplaining' - it endures neglect.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The writer's final point is that the barn had a value that was
questions.A: purely financial, like the uncle's cassava
questions.B: recorded carefully in the family's account book
questions.C: greater than the value of the land it stood on
questions.D: social and emotional, not merely financial
questions.explanation: 'Something went with the barn that was not measured in naira' - the family gathering, pride and visible security.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: According to the first paragraph, over short distances in city traffic a bicycle is
questions.A: slower but cheaper than a bus
questions.B: faster than a car or a bus
questions.C: exactly as fast as a car
questions.D: the most expensive of the three options
questions.explanation: 'Over any distance under five kilometres in city traffic, faster than either a car or a bus.'

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The writer thinks the most important reason Nigerians avoid bicycles is
questions.A: the heat and the heavy rain
questions.B: the danger from lorries on the roads
questions.D: the poor quality of the bicycles sold
questions.explanation: 'But the largest part, I suspect, is status... to be seen on one is to announce that one cannot afford anything better.'

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The example of Amsterdam and Copenhagen is used to show that
questions.A: bankers in Europe are poorer than bankers in Nigeria
questions.B: cycling has always been popular in European cities
questions.C: European cities enjoy far better weather than Lagos
questions.D: attitudes to cycling can change in a generation
questions.explanation: 'Forty years ago the same was true... until a generation decided otherwise.'

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The expression 'articulated lorries' as used in the passage refers to
questions.A: lorries that make a very loud noise
questions.B: large lorries built in two jointed sections
questions.D: small delivery vans used by traders
questions.explanation: An articulated lorry has a cab and a trailer joined by a pivot; the point is their size and danger to cyclists.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the last two sentences the writer suggests that
questions.A: the weather must change before people will cycle
questions.B: only the government can change anything about it
questions.C: both government and citizens have a part to play
questions.D: the problem cannot be solved in Nigerian cities
questions.explanation: Safe lanes are 'the government's job'; being seen to prefer the bicycle 'is ours'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The new stadium cost the state an arm and a leg.
questions.A: The stadium was paid for by the athletes
questions.B: The stadium was built by injured workers
questions.C: The stadium was finished very quickly
questions.explanation: To 'cost an arm and a leg' is to cost a great deal of money.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Ngozi visits her village once in a blue moon.
questions.A: Ngozi visits her village every month
questions.B: Ngozi visits her village very rarely
questions.C: Ngozi visits her village only at night
questions.D: Ngozi visits her village when the moon is full
questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Stop beating about the bush and tell me what happened.
questions.A: Stop shouting and lower your voice
questions.B: Stop cutting the hedge and come inside
questions.C: Stop avoiding the point and speak plainly
questions.D: Stop lying and admit your mistake
questions.explanation: 'Beat about the bush' is to avoid coming to the point.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Since the factory closed, all the workers are in the same boat.
questions.A: The workers have all found new jobs at the same place
questions.B: The workers have all gone fishing on the same boat
questions.C: The workers are all travelling home together by boat
questions.D: The workers are all in the same difficult situation
questions.explanation: 'In the same boat' means facing the same unpleasant situation.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: When Mr Ojo blamed poor planning, he hit the nail on the head.
questions.A: Mr Ojo injured himself while repairing the building
questions.B: Mr Ojo identified the exact cause of the problem
questions.C: Mr Ojo lost his temper with the planning committee
questions.D: Mr Ojo blamed the wrong people for the failure
questions.explanation: To 'hit the nail on the head' is to describe a situation exactly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Amaka has been feeling under the weather since Monday.
questions.A: Amaka has been very cheerful since Monday
questions.B: Amaka has been caught in the rain since Monday
questions.C: Amaka has been slightly ill since Monday
questions.D: Amaka has been working outdoors since Monday
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' means unwell.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The team threw in the towel with ten minutes left.
questions.A: The team protested to the referee
questions.B: The team changed its kit before the match ended
questions.C: The team scored a late goal
questions.D: The team gave up before the match ended
questions.explanation: 'Throw in the towel' means to admit defeat.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: To add insult to injury, the driver demanded extra fare after the breakdown.
questions.A: The driver apologised for the breakdown
questions.B: The driver made a bad situation even worse
questions.C: The driver was injured in the breakdown
questions.D: The driver abused the injured passengers
questions.explanation: 'Add insult to injury' is to make a bad situation worse by a further wrong.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The third late delivery was the last straw for the customer.
questions.A: The customer was pleased that the delivery finally came
questions.B: The customer ordered drinking straws for the third time
questions.C: The final problem that made the customer lose patience
questions.D: The delivery arrived without any of its packaging
questions.explanation: 'The last straw' is the final difficulty that makes a situation unbearable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Their donation was a drop in the ocean compared to what the hospital needs.
questions.A: Their donation was larger than expected
questions.B: Their donation was made to a hospital by the sea
questions.C: Their donation was lost in transit
questions.D: Their donation was very small beside what is needed
questions.explanation: 'A drop in the ocean' is a very small amount compared with what is needed.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: By studying on the bus, Tunde kills two birds with one stone.
questions.A: Tunde throws stones at birds on his way to school
questions.B: Tunde achieves two aims with a single action
questions.C: Tunde is careless with his time on the way to school
questions.D: Tunde disturbs the other passengers with his books
questions.explanation: 'Kill two birds with one stone' is to achieve two things with one effort.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: With prices rising, many families struggle to make ends meet.
questions.A: Many families cannot agree with one another about prices
questions.B: Many families are moving to the far ends of the town
questions.C: Many families barely have enough money for necessities
questions.D: Many families are managing to save a great deal of money
questions.explanation: 'Make ends meet' is to have just enough money to live on.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Ade got cold feet on the morning of the wedding.
questions.A: Ade fell ill with a fever on the morning of the wedding
questions.B: Ade had no shoes to wear to his own wedding
questions.C: Ade arrived at the wedding venue far too early
questions.D: Ade became nervous and unwilling to go ahead
questions.explanation: 'Get cold feet' is to lose one's nerve about a planned action.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The fire service arrived in the nick of time.
questions.A: The fire service arrived far too late to be of any help
questions.B: The fire service arrived just before it was too late
questions.C: The fire service arrived with a badly damaged engine
questions.D: The fire service arrived at the wrong address entirely
questions.explanation: 'In the nick of time' means at the last possible moment.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Take the agent's promises with a pinch of salt.
questions.A: Write the agent's promises down carefully
questions.B: Reward the agent with a gift of salt
questions.C: Do not believe the agent's promises entirely
questions.D: Accept the agent's promises with gratitude
questions.explanation: To take something 'with a pinch of salt' is to doubt that it is completely true.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The contractor took the lion's share of the profit.
questions.A: The contractor refused to take any part of the profit
questions.B: The contractor spent the profit on a visit to the zoo
questions.C: The contractor shared the profit equally with the workers
questions.D: The contractor took the largest part of the profit
questions.explanation: 'The lion's share' is the biggest portion.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Reading between the lines, the letter is a refusal.
questions.A: The letter is written on ruled paper in small print
questions.B: The hidden meaning of the letter is a refusal
questions.C: The letter has been read too quickly to be understood
questions.D: The letter openly and plainly refuses the request
questions.explanation: 'Read between the lines' is to find a meaning that is implied, not stated.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Little did Chike know that the letter had already been posted.
questions.A: Chike posted the letter himself without telling anyone
questions.B: Chike knew only a little about the letter's contents
questions.C: Chike had no idea that the letter had been posted
questions.D: Chike read only a small part of the letter
questions.explanation: 'Little did he know' means he was completely unaware.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Were it not for the goalkeeper, the team would have lost.
questions.A: The goalkeeper did not play in the match
questions.B: The goalkeeper caused the team to lose
questions.C: The team lost despite the goalkeeper
questions.D: The goalkeeper saved the team from defeat
questions.explanation: 'Were it not for X' means 'if X had not been there' - the goalkeeper prevented the loss.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Bisi is nothing if not punctual.
questions.C: Bisi is punctual only when it suits her
questions.D: Bisi is nothing more than punctual
questions.explanation: 'Nothing if not' emphasises a quality: she is above all punctual.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Uncle Sam is no fool when it comes to money.
questions.A: Uncle Sam wastes his money foolishly
questions.B: Uncle Sam has no money at all
questions.C: Uncle Sam is very shrewd about money
questions.D: Uncle Sam refuses to talk about money
questions.explanation: 'No fool' means very sensible or clever.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The typewriter has become OBSOLETE in modern offices.
questions.explanation: Obsolete means no longer in use because something newer exists.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The auditor was METICULOUS in checking every receipt.
questions.explanation: Meticulous means very careful and precise.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The school plans to AUGMENT its library with new books.
questions.explanation: To augment is to increase or add to.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: There is a DEARTH of qualified teachers in rural areas.
questions.explanation: A dearth is a scarcity or lack.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The charity provides food for INDIGENT families.
questions.explanation: Indigent means very poor, needy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The VOCIFEROUS protesters could be heard from the next street.
questions.explanation: Vociferous means loud and forceful in expressing views.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The chief's OSTENTATIOUS display of wealth annoyed the villagers.
questions.explanation: Ostentatious means designed to impress or attract notice.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The hot afternoon made the students LETHARGIC.
questions.explanation: Lethargic means lacking energy, drowsy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The lawyer asked only PERTINENT questions.
questions.explanation: Pertinent means directly related to the matter in hand.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: Power supply in the area is SPORADIC.
questions.explanation: Sporadic means occurring at irregular intervals.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The dispute began over a TRIVIAL matter.
questions.explanation: Trivial means of little value or importance.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: She is a ZEALOUS supporter of the campaign.
questions.explanation: Zealous means full of energy and eagerness for a cause.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The OBSTINATE boy refused to apologise.
questions.explanation: Obstinate means stubbornly refusing to change one's mind.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The AFFLUENT suburb has wide, tree-lined streets.
questions.explanation: Affluent means having a great deal of money.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: New evidence EXONERATED the accused man.
questions.explanation: To exonerate is to free someone from blame.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The manager tried to PLACATE the angry customers.
questions.explanation: To placate is to make someone less angry.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: He SQUANDERED his inheritance within two years.
questions.explanation: To squander is to waste money recklessly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The INCESSANT noise from the road kept us awake.
questions.explanation: Incessant means continuing without pause.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: Climbing the mountain proved an ARDUOUS task.
questions.explanation: Arduous means requiring great effort.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The report VINDICATED the doctor's decision.
questions.explanation: To vindicate is to show that something was right or justified.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The bridge is only a TEMPORARY structure.
questions.explanation: Temporary (lasting a short time) is the opposite of permanent.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The meaning of the poem is OBSCURE.
questions.explanation: Obscure (unclear) is the opposite of clear.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The NEGLIGENT nurse forgot to record the dose.
questions.explanation: Negligent (careless) is the opposite of careful.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: She has a PROFOUND knowledge of history.
questions.explanation: Profound (deep) is the opposite of superficial (shallow).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: His EXTRAVAGANT spending worried his parents.
questions.explanation: Extravagant (wasteful) is the opposite of thrifty (economical).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The new engine will ACCELERATE the process.
questions.explanation: Accelerate is the opposite of slow down.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The ARROGANT official refused to listen to the farmers.
questions.explanation: Arrogant (proud, overbearing) is the opposite of humble.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The court found the man INNOCENT.
questions.explanation: Innocent is the opposite of guilty.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: He remained cheerful in ADVERSITY.
questions.explanation: Adversity (misfortune) is the opposite of prosperity.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Bola is always PUNCTUAL for lectures.
questions.explanation: Punctual (on time) is the opposite of late.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The scene at the motor park was CHAOTIC.
questions.explanation: Chaotic (in complete disorder) is the opposite of orderly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The speaker's VERBOSE address bored the audience.
questions.explanation: Verbose (using too many words) is the opposite of concise.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The doctor said the growth was BENIGN.
questions.explanation: Benign (not harmful) is the opposite of malignant.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The land around the mine is STERILE.
questions.explanation: Sterile (unable to produce crops) is the opposite of fertile.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The MALICIOUS rumour ruined her reputation.
questions.explanation: Malicious (intending harm) is the opposite of benevolent (kindly).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: As a NOVICE, he made many mistakes.
questions.explanation: A novice (beginner) is the opposite of an expert.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The RIGID rules allowed no exceptions.
questions.explanation: Rigid (unbending) is the opposite of flexible.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The village was TRANQUIL at dawn.
questions.explanation: Tranquil (peaceful) is the opposite of noisy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The shop sells ARTIFICIAL flowers.
questions.explanation: Artificial (man-made) is the opposite of natural.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The road began to DETERIORATE after the floods.
questions.explanation: Deteriorate (get worse) is the opposite of improve.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Mathematics ____ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -s (mathematics, physics, economics) take a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Either the students or the teacher ____ responsible for the noise.
questions.explanation: With 'either... or' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the teacher'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She speaks English ____ than her brother.
questions.explanation: An adverb of manner ('fluently') forms its comparative with 'more'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: This is the ____ book I have ever read.
questions.explanation: 'The... I have ever' requires the superlative: 'most interesting'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: He has very ____ friends, so he is often lonely.
questions.explanation: 'Friends' is countable, so 'few' (not 'little') is used.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: There is ____ milk left in the fridge, so buy some.
questions.explanation: 'Milk' is uncountable, so 'little' is used; 'little' (not 'a little') stresses the shortage.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I have not seen Musa ____ last Christmas.
questions.explanation: 'Since' marks the starting point of a period that continues to now.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The meeting has been postponed ____ next Tuesday.
questions.explanation: Something is postponed until (up to) a later time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Funke is married ____ a doctor from Ilorin.
questions.explanation: One is married to a person, not 'with'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The clerk was accused ____ stealing the money.
questions.explanation: 'Accused of' is the correct collocation ('charged with', but 'accused of').

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The chairman objected ____ the new proposal.
questions.explanation: 'Object to' is the correct preposition.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The novel consists ____ twelve chapters.
questions.explanation: 'Consist of' means to be made up of.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: We arrived ____ Lagos shortly after noon.
questions.explanation: 'Arrive in' is used for cities and countries; 'arrive at' for smaller places or buildings.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The teacher shared the sweets ____ the five children.
questions.explanation: 'Among' is used for more than two; 'between' for two.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: If Ada had studied harder, she ____ the examination.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: 'if' + past perfect, 'would have' + past participle.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I wish it ____ raining so that we could go out.
questions.explanation: 'Wish' + 'would' expresses a desire for a change in the present situation.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: By the time you arrive, we ____ dinner.
questions.explanation: The future perfect describes an action completed before a future time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The letters ____ yesterday, so they should arrive tomorrow.
questions.explanation: A finished past action with a time adverb ('yesterday') takes the simple past passive.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: He asked me whether I ____ the film before.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after 'asked', the present perfect becomes the past perfect.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: You ____ better see a doctor about that cough.
questions.explanation: 'Had better' + bare infinitive is the fixed expression for advice.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: ____ he is very rich, he is not happy.
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces a clause; 'despite' and 'in spite of' take a noun or -ing form.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The reason he failed is ____ he did not read.
questions.explanation: 'The reason... is that' is the accepted construction; 'the reason is because' is faulty.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: It was ____ hot day that we could not go out.
questions.explanation: 'Such a' + adjective + noun; 'so' is followed directly by an adjective.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Amina is ____ honest girl.
questions.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (the 'h' is silent), so 'an' is used.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: One of the boys ____ broken the window.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The information you gave me ____ very useful.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Ten thousand naira ____ not enough for the rent.
questions.explanation: A sum of money regarded as a single amount takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Kemi ____ in Kano for ten years before she moved to Jos.
questions.explanation: The past perfect shows the earlier of two past actions.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The teacher made us ____ the passage aloud.
questions.explanation: 'Make' + object + bare infinitive (without 'to') in the active voice.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Ayo avoided ____ to his uncle after the quarrel.
questions.explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by the -ing form.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Everyone except Tunde ____ arrived.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is singular; the phrase 'except Tunde' does not change the number.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Would you mind ____ the window?
questions.explanation: 'Mind' is followed by the -ing form.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): university
questions.explanation: u-ni-VER-si-ty - words ending in '-ity' are stressed on the syllable before '-ity'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): important
questions.explanation: im-POR-tant - stress on the second syllable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): engineer
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-eer' are stressed on that ending: en-gi-NEER.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): competition
questions.explanation: '-tion' words are stressed on the syllable before the ending: com-pe-TI-tion.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): certificate
questions.explanation: cer-TI-fi-cate - stress on the second syllable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): information
questions.explanation: '-tion' words are stressed on the preceding syllable: in-for-MA-tion.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): hospital
questions.explanation: HOS-pi-tal - stress on the first syllable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): independent
questions.explanation: in-de-PEN-dent - stress on the third syllable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): calculator
questions.explanation: CAL-cu-la-tor - stress on the first syllable, as in 'calculate'.
